claim: Genome instability in yeast and mammals is caused by RNA–DNA hybrids that form as a result of defects in different aspects of RNA biogenesis.
source: Genome instability in yeast and mammals is caused by RNA–DNA hybrids that form as a result of defects in different aspects of RNA biogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Huertas and Aguilera, 2003; Li and Manley, 2005; Kim and Jinks-Robertson, 2009; Paulsen et al., 2009; Wahba et al., 2011; Stirling et al., 2012) as mentioned in the Introduction.

claim: In yeast mutants defective for transcription repression and RNA degradation, hybrid formation requires Rad51p and Rad52p.
source: We report that in yeast mutants defective for transcription repression and RNA degradation, hybrid formation requires Rad51p and Rad52p.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 7, where deletion of RAD51 or RAD52 suppresses hybrid formation in RNA biogenesis mutants.

claim: Rad51p and Rad52p normally promote DNA–DNA strand exchange in homologous recombination.
source: These proteins normally promote DNA–DNA strand exchange in homologous recombination.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the canonical function of Rad51p and Rad52p.

claim: Rad51p and Rad52p directly promote the DNA–RNA strand exchange necessary for hybrid formation.
source: We suggest they also directly promote the DNA–RNA strand exchange necessary for hybrid formation since we observed accumulation of Rad51p at a model hybrid-forming locus.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observation of Rad51p accumulation at hybrid-forming loci (Figure 3).

claim: Rad51p accumulates at a model hybrid-forming locus.
source: we observed accumulation of Rad51p at a model hybrid-forming locus.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 3A demonstrating Rad51p binding to the YAC-GALpr locus upon galactose induction.

claim: Rad51p mediates hybridization of transcripts to homologous chromosomal loci distinct from their site of synthesis.
source: Furthermore, we provide evidence that Rad51p mediates hybridization of transcripts to homologous chromosomal loci distinct from their site of synthesis.
evidence: This is supported by the trans hybrid formation experiments shown in Figures 5 and 6, where transcription from chromosome III causes hybrid formation on the YAC.

claim: Hybrid formation in trans amplifies the genome-destabilizing potential of RNA.
source: This hybrid formation in trans amplifies the genome-destabilizing potential of RNA and broadens the exclusive co-transcriptional models that pervade the field.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that trans hybrid formation can cause instability at sites distant from transcription.

claim: The deleterious hybrid-forming activity of Rad51p is counteracted by Srs2p.
source: The deleterious hybrid-forming activity of Rad51p is counteracted by Srs2p, a known Rad51p antagonist.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8 showing that srs2Δ increases hybrid formation and YAC instability in a Rad51p-dependent manner.

claim: Srs2p is a known Rad51p antagonist.
source: Srs2p, a known Rad51p antagonist.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Srs2p function, as referenced in the manuscript (Krejci et al., 2003).

claim: Srs2p serves as a novel anti-hybrid mechanism in vivo.
source: Thus Srs2p serves as a novel anti-hybrid mechanism in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that deletion of SRS2 increases hybrid formation.

claim: Less than 5% of wild-type nuclei stain with S9.6 antibody.
source: As reported previously, less than 5% of wild-type nuclei stain with this antibody (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from chromosome spreads shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 80–85% of nuclei in RNA biogenesis mutants show robust S9.6 staining.
source: In contrast, 80–85% of nuclei in our representative set of RNA biogenesis mutants showed robust staining, indicating the formation of stable hybrids at many loci in most cells (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from chromosome spreads shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Deletion of RAD51 in RNA biogenesis mutants diminishes S9.6 staining threefold to fourfold to near background levels.
source: The deletion of RAD51 (rad51Δ) in these mutants diminished S9.6 staining in nearly all nuclei from the RNA biogenesis mutants threefold to fourfold to near background levels (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from chromosome spreads comparing RNA biogenesis mutants with and without rad51Δ.

claim: S9.6 binding to sin3Δ nucleic acids is elevated approximately tenfold relative to sin3Δ rad51Δ.
source: S9.6 binding to sin3Δ nucleic acids was elevated approximately tenfold relative to sin3Δ rad51Δ (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by dot blot analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The total rate of YAC instability in wild-type cells is 6 × 10−4 per division.
source: The total rate of YAC instability (the sum of chromosome loss and terminal deletions) in wild-type cells was 6 × 10−4 per division.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the YAC instability assay.

claim: rad51Δ alone causes no increase in YAC instability.
source: Notably, rad51Δ alone caused no increase in YAC instability.
evidence: This is supported by the YAC instability data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: YAC instability increases fivefold to tenfold in RNA biogenesis mutants.
source: In our subset of RNA biogenesis mutants, YAC instability increased fivefold to tenfold (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative YAC instability measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Introduction of rad51Δ into RNA biogenesis mutants completely suppresses elevated YAC instability in leo1Δ, kem1Δ, rrp6Δ, and sin3Δ mutants.
source: The introduction of rad51Δ into the RNA biogenesis mutants completely suppressed the elevated YAC instability, both chromosome loss and terminal deletions, in leo1Δ, kem1Δ, rrp6Δ, and sin3Δ mutants.
evidence: This is supported by YAC instability data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In med12Δ, YAC instability is mostly but not entirely suppressed by rad51Δ despite near complete suppression of hybrid formation.
source: In med12Δ, YAC instability was mostly but not entirely suppressed despite the near complete suppression of hybrid formation as monitored by spreads, indicating that in the med12Δ rad51Δ strain a subset of the YAC instability was hybrid independent.
evidence: This is based on comparison of hybrid staining and YAC instability data for med12Δ rad51Δ shown in Figure 1.

claim: Addition of galactose to YAC-GALpr induces approximately one hundredfold induction of RNA at least 1 kb on both sides of the GAL promoter.
source: This analysis revealed approximately one hundredfold induction of RNA at least 1 kb on both sides of the GAL promoter (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A dramatic increase in DIP signal for hybrids occurs on YAC sequences proximal to YAC-GALpr 2 hr after induction by galactose.
source: In contrast, we observed a dramatic increase in the DIP signal for hybrids on the YAC sequences proximal to YAC-GALpr, 2 hr after induction by galactose (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by DIP analysis data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No elevation in hybrid signal is detected in two regions of the YAC-GALpr distal to the GALpr.
source: The specificity of this increased DIP signal was evident by the fact that no elevation in hybrid signal was detected in two regions of the YAC-GALpr distal to the GALpr (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by DIP analysis at distal regions shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Lower DIP signals coincide with the transcriptional start site of the GALpr where there is little transcript detectable upon addition of galactose.
source: Additionally, lower DIP signals coincide with the transcriptional start site of the GALpr, where there is little transcript detectable upon addition of galactose (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on correlation of DIP signals with transcript levels shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: The DIP signal in YAC-GALpr strains is suppressed when transcription is repressed by the addition of glucose.
source: Furthermore, the DIP signal in the YAC-GALpr strains was suppressed when transcription was repressed by the addition of glucose (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by DIP analysis after glucose addition shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: YAC-GALpr instability is elevated 25-fold upon galactose treatment.
source: Indeed, its instability was elevated 25-fold with a distribution of chromosome loss and terminal deletions similar to that seen in wild-type cells and RNA biogenesis mutants (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by YAC instability measurements shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: Transcription-induced YAC instability is suppressed by over-expression of RNase H.
source: Furthermore, this transcription-induced YAC instability was suppressed by over-expression of RNase H or deletion of RAD51 (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This is supported by YAC instability data with RNase H overexpression shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Transcription-induced YAC instability is suppressed by deletion of RAD51.
source: Furthermore, this transcription-induced YAC instability was suppressed by over-expression of RNase H or deletion of RAD51 (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This is supported by YAC instability data in rad51Δ shown in Figure 2E.

claim: No Rad51p binding is detected on YAC-GALpr in the absence of galactose.
source: No Rad51p binding was detected either on YAC-GALpr in the absence of galactose or on the YAC in the presence or absence of galactose (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Significant Rad51p binding is detected around the GAL promoter on YAC-GALpr upon addition of galactose and induction of transcription.
source: In contrast, using either antibody for ChIP, significant Rad51p binding was detected around the GAL promoter on YAC-GALpr upon the addition of galactose and induction of transcription (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data using both anti-HA and polyclonal anti-Rad51p antibodies shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Rad51p binding appears to extend further than the region of hybrid formation detected by DIP.
source: Notably, Rad51p binding appears to extend further than the region of hybrid formation detected by DIP (Figure 2C and Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on comparison of ChIP and DIP data shown in Figures 2C and 3A.

claim: Rad51p is known to spread from regions of ssDNA into dsDNA.
source: Rad51p is known to spread from regions of ssDNA into dsDNA (Zaitsev and Kowalczykowski, 2000), and it is possible that in our model locus Rad51p is spreading from the ssDNA or RNA–DNA hybrid into the neighboring dsDNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Rad51p behavior supported by citation.

claim: Rad51p binding disappears when galactose-induced YAC-GALpr transcription is repressed by addition of dextrose.
source: In these cultures, Rad51p binding disappeared (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data after dextrose addition shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: No significant change in γ-H2a.X signal is detected within 2 hr of galactose induction in YAC-GALpr.
source: However, we did not detect a ChIP signal for γ-H2AX above background level in the YAC-GALpr strain even under conditions that induced Rad51p binding (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by γ-H2AX ChIP data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: No increase in YAC instability is observed when dextrose is added after 2 hr of galactose induction.
source: However, no increase in YAC instability was observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), indicating that binding of Rad51p to this locus during the first 2 hr was unlikely to result from DNA damage.
evidence: This is supported by YAC instability data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Neither hybrid staining nor YAC instability is suppressed in rnh1Δrnh201Δ rad51Δ compared to rnh1Δrnh201Δ.
source: To test whether these naturally occurring hybrids are also dependent on Rad51p, we monitored hybrid staining and YAC instability in rnh1Δrnh201Δ in the absence of RAD51. Neither hybrid staining nor YAC instability was suppressed (Figure 4A,B), indicating that the transient hybrids in wild-type cells are not Rad51p dependent.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A and 4B comparing rnh1Δrnh201Δ with and without rad51Δ.

claim: Transient hybrids in wild-type cells are not Rad51p dependent.
source: Neither hybrid staining nor YAC instability was suppressed (Figure 4A,B), indicating that the transient hybrids in wild-type cells are not Rad51p dependent.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that rad51Δ does not suppress hybrids in rnh1Δrnh201Δ.

claim: Both Rad51p-dependent and -independent mechanisms for hybrid formation exist.
source: Thus both Rad51p-dependent and -independent mechanisms for hybrid formation exist.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential effects of rad51Δ on hybrids in different mutant backgrounds.

claim: A strong DIP signal is generated by primers monitoring hybrids from both YAC and YAC-GALpr module only in the presence of galactose.
source: One primer set that monitored hybrids from both the YAC and YAC-GALpr module generated a strong DIP signal only in the presence of galactose (Figure 5B, primer 1).
evidence: This is supported by DIP analysis data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The combined hybrid signal from YAC and YAC-GALpr module is eliminated when rad51Δ is introduced.
source: This combined hybrid signal was eliminated when the rad51Δ was introduced in this strain (Figure 5B, primer 1).
evidence: This is supported by DIP analysis in rad51Δ background shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Primers monitoring hybrids only from the YAC reveal a strong DIP signal only in the presence of galactose.
source: Two other primer sets that monitored hybrids only from the YAC also revealed a strong DIP signal only in the presence of galactose (Figure 5B, primers 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by DIP analysis data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The trans-specific hybrid signal is eliminated when rad51Δ is introduced.
source: This trans-specific hybrid signal was eliminated when rad51Δ was introduced into our strain.
evidence: This is supported by DIP analysis in rad51Δ background shown in Figure 5B.

claim: No increase in YAC instability is observed in LW7003 strain in the absence of galactose.
source: As expected, no increase in YAC instability was observed in this strain in the absence of galactose (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by YAC instability data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: YAC instability increases tenfold upon galactose-induced transcription of the YAC-GALpr module on chromosome III.
source: However, YAC instability increased tenfold upon galactose-induced transcription of the YAC-GALpr module on chromosome III (Figure 6A, black bars).
evidence: This is supported by YAC instability measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Transcription-induced YAC instability is dependent on homology between the YAC and transcribed YAC sequences from the YAC-GALpr module on chromosome III.
source: The transcription-induced YAC instability was dependent on the homology between the YAC and the transcribed YAC sequences from the YAC-GALpr module on chromosome III, as deletion of the corresponding 1 kb of homology from the YAC completely suppressed the transcription-induced YAC instability (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by YAC instability data when homology is deleted shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Elevated YAC instability from trans transcription is blocked by RNase H over-expression.
source: The elevated YAC instability was blocked by RNase H over-expression, indicating the YAC instability was hybrid dependent (Figure 6A, gray bars).
evidence: This is supported by YAC instability data with RNase H overexpression shown in Figure 6A.

claim: YAC instability from trans transcription is blocked by introduction of rad51Δ in LW7003.
source: YAC instability was also blocked after introduction of the rad51Δ in LW7003 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by YAC instability data in rad51Δ background shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Hybrids induced in trans and in cis both lead to a similar distribution of YAC instability events with on average 85% HIS− URA− and 15% HIS+ URA−.
source: Indeed hybrids induced in trans and in cis both lead to a similar distribution of YAC instability events; on average 85% are HIS− URA− (chromosome loss) and 15% are HIS+ URA− (putative terminal deletions).
evidence: This is based on analysis of YAC instability events in both cis and trans systems.

claim: The total rate of YAC instability increases only 10-fold by hybrids formed in trans compared to 25-fold by hybrids formed in cis.
source: However, the total rate of YAC instability increased only 10-fold by hybrids formed in trans (from the YAC-GALpr module on chromosome III) compared to 25-fold by hybrids formed in cis.
evidence: This is based on comparison of YAC instability rates in trans (Figure 6) versus cis (Figure 2) systems.

claim: Hybrid formation in trans may be less efficient than in cis.
source: Thus, hybrid formation in trans may be less efficient than in cis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lower fold-increase in YAC instability observed in trans versus cis.

claim: Nine out of ten analyzed YAC rearrangements in LW7003 are shorter than the existing YAC, consistent with YAC terminal deletions.
source: Amongst the 10 YAC rearrangements analyzed, nine were shorter than the existing YAC, consistent with the formation of YAC terminal deletions (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by pulse-field gel and Southern analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Only one out of ten YAC rearrangements in LW7003 is the size expected for a chromosome III;YAC translocation.
source: Only one rearrangement was the size expected if a chromosome III;YAC translocation had occurred.
evidence: This is based on pulse-field gel and Southern analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Deletion of RAD52 in RNA biogenesis mutants completely suppresses hybrid staining.
source: Deletion of RAD52 (rad52Δ) in our panel of transcriptional mutants completely suppressed hybrid staining, as assayed by chromosome spreads (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by chromosome spread data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Rad52p is required for the binding of Rad51p to ssDNA.
source: Rad52p is required for the binding of Rad51p to ssDNA (Figure 7A; Song and Sung, 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Song and Sung, 2000.

claim: Hybrid formation is not simply a consequence of rogue activity by Rad51p but occurs as part of the canonical Rad51p repair pathway.
source: Nonetheless, the suppression of hybrid staining by rad52Δ suggests that hybrid formation is not simply a consequence of rogue activity by Rad51p but rather occurs as part of the canonical Rad51p repair pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the requirement for Rad52p, a canonical Rad51p cofactor, for hybrid formation.

claim: Neither single nor double deletions of RAD54 and RDH54 significantly increase hybrid formation or YAC instability.
source: Neither single nor double deletions of RAD54 and RDH54 significantly increased hybrid formation or YAC instability (Figure 8A,B, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by YAC instability and hybrid staining data shown in Figure 8A, B, and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deletion of SRS2 increases both hybrid staining and YAC instability.
source: In contrast, deletion of SRS2 increased both hybrid staining and YAC instability.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8A, B, and C.

claim: Both hybrid staining and YAC instability phenotypes of srs2Δ are suppressed in srs2Δ rad51Δ mutant.
source: Both of these phenotypes of the srs2Δ were suppressed in the srs2Δ rad51Δ mutant (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8C comparing srs2Δ with srs2Δ rad51Δ.

claim: Srs2p antagonizes the hybrid-forming activity of the Rad51p pathway.
source: Thus, Srs2p antagonizes the hybrid-forming activity of the Rad51p pathway and represents another mechanism by which cells protect their genome against hybrid formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that srs2Δ increases hybrids in a Rad51p-dependent manner.

claim: The hybrid staining pattern in srs2Δ nuclei exhibits an apparent enrichment of RNA–DNA hybrids at the RDN locus on chromosome XII.
source: The hybrid staining pattern in srs2Δ nuclei was reminiscent of the pattern observed in sin3Δ cells, exhibiting an apparent enrichment of RNA–DNA hybrids at the RDN locus on chromosome XII, the site of 150 tandem rDNA copies (Wahba et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on visual inspection of hybrid staining patterns and comparison to previous observations.

claim: In srs2Δ cells, the rate of rDNA instability is twenty threefold greater compared to wild-type cells.
source: In srs2Δ cells, the rate of rDNA instability is twenty threefold greater compared to wild-type cells, a marked increase in instability as compared to the fourfold increase in YAC instability (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: This is supported by rDNA instability measurements shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Srs2p has a particularly important role in protecting the highly transcribed rDNA locus against Rad51p-dependent hybrid formation and repeat instability.
source: Together these results suggest that Srs2p has a particularly important role in protecting the highly transcribed rDNA locus against Rad51p-dependent hybrid formation and repeat instability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the disproportionately high rDNA instability in srs2Δ compared to YAC instability.

claim: RecA promotes RNA–DNA hybrid formation in vitro.
source: Studies a decade ago showed that RecA promotes RNA–DNA hybrid formation in vitro (Kasahara et al., 2000; Zaitsev and Kowalczykowski, 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior in vitro studies supported by citations.

claim: RecA-mediated R-loops can form when RecA is mixed with RNA and its homologous DNA template in the absence of active transcription.
source: In these studies, RecA-mediated R-loops formed when RecA was mixed with RNA and its homologous DNA template in the absence of active transcription.
evidence: This is based on prior in vitro studies with RecA cited in the manuscript.

claim: Hybrids can form post-transcriptionally (in trans) at least in vitro.
source: This observation showed that hybrids could, at least in vitro, form post-transcriptionally (i.e., in trans) (Kasahara et al., 2000; Zaitsev and Kowalczykowski, 2000).
evidence: This is based on interpretation of prior in vitro RecA studies.

claim: Models from in vivo studies suggest that RNA–DNA hybrids occur co-transcriptionally (in cis) from invasion of duplex DNA at the site of transcription by a nascent RNA transcript.
source: However, to date, models postulated from in vivo studies suggest that RNA–DNA hybrids occur co-transcriptionally (in cis) from the invasion of the duplex DNA at the site of transcription by a nascent RNA transcript (Huertas and Aguilera, 2003; Aguilera and García-Muse, 2012).
evidence: This is a summary of prevailing models in the field supported by citations.

claim: The cis mechanism is supported by the co-transcriptional nature of many RNA biogenesis steps implicated in preventing hybrid formation.
source: The cis mechanism is supported by the co-transcriptional nature of many of the RNA biogenesis steps implicated in preventing hybrid formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known co-transcriptional nature of RNA biogenesis factors.

claim: The cis mechanism does not fully explain how mutants in post-transcriptional processes such as RNA degradation and export would cause hybrid-mediated instability.
source: However, the cis mechanism does not fully explain how mutants in post-transcriptional processes, such as RNA degradation and export, would cause hybrid-mediated instability (Wahba et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the timing of post-transcriptional processes relative to transcription.

claim: Levels of RNA–DNA hybrids increase when RNA biogenesis is disturbed at sites of transcription initiation or repression, elongation, splicing, degradation, and export.
source: Genome-wide screens in budding yeast and human cells have revealed that levels of RNA–DNA hybrids increase when RNA biogenesis is disturbed at sites of transcription initiation or repression, elongation, splicing, degradation, and export (Huertas and Aguilera, 2003; Li and Manley, 2005; Paulsen et al., 2009; Wahba et al., 2011; Stirling et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from genome-wide screens supported by multiple citations.

claim: RNA biogenesis factors prevent hybrid formation by restricting access of nascent RNA molecules to the DNA template at the site of transcription.
source: The co-transcriptional binding of many RNA processing and transcription factors suggests that they prevent hybrid formation by restricting the access of nascent RNA molecules to the DNA template at the site of transcription (Aguilera and García-Muse, 2012).
evidence: This is a mechanistic model based on the co-transcriptional binding of RNA biogenesis factors, supported by citation.

claim: Hybrids form transiently at some loci in wild-type budding yeast but are removed rapidly by hybrid removal factors including two endogenous RNase H enzymes and Sen1p.
source: Recent studies suggest that these RNA biogenesis factors are not sufficient to prevent transient hybrid formation at some loci in wild-type budding yeast; rather, hybrids form but are removed rapidly by hybrid removal factors, including two endogenous RNase H enzymes, and Sen1p, an RNA–DNA helicase (Mischo et al., 2011; Wahba et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on recent studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: In RNA biogenesis mutants, elevated levels of hybrid formation overwhelm the capacity of hybrid removal factors, allowing accumulation of hybrids and genome instability.
source: In RNA biogenesis mutants the elevated levels of hybrid formation overwhelm the capacity of these hybrid removal factors, allowing the accumulation of hybrids and genome instability.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model to explain hybrid accumulation in RNA biogenesis mutants.

claim: RNA polymerase generates negative supercoiling behind the elongating polymerase which facilitates DNA unwinding and may allow RNA access to the DNA template.
source: One potential factor is RNA polymerase, which generates negative supercoiling behind the elongating polymerase. The negative supercoiling facilitates DNA unwinding, and may allow RNA access to the DNA template (Roy et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis based on the known properties of RNA polymerase and supported by citation.

claim: A connection between negative supercoiling and hybrid formation is supported by in vivo work on topoisomerase mutants in bacteria, yeast, and human cells.
source: A connection between negative supercoiling and hybrid formation is supported by in vivo work on topoisomerase mutants in bacteria, yeast, and human cells (Drolet et al., 1995; Tuduri et al., 2009; El Hage et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by prior studies on topoisomerase mutants cited in the manuscript.

claim: Over-expressing Rad51p can compromise genome integrity.
source: Interestingly, previous in vivo studies showed that over-expressing Rad51p can compromise genome integrity (Richardson et al., 2004; Shah et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies supported by citations.

claim: Instability from Rad51p overexpression may result in part from the ability of Rad51p to promote RNA–DNA hybrid formation.
source: We suggest that this instability may result in part from the ability of Rad51p to promote RNA–DNA hybrid formation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of prior observations in light of the current findings.

claim: RAD51 expression is up-regulated in tumor cells.
source: This deleterious activity of Rad51p is also intriguing because a number of studies have shown that RAD51 expression is up-regulated in tumor cells (Klein, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cancer biology supported by citation.

claim: High levels of Rad51p in tumor cells have been interpreted as evidence for Rad51p acting as a tumor suppressor by ensuring non-faulty repair of DNA damage.
source: These high levels of Rad51p have been interpreted as evidence for Rad51p acting as a tumor suppressor by ensuring non-faulty repair of DNA damage.
evidence: This is a summary of a prevailing interpretation in the field.

claim: High levels of Rad51p may be oncogenic, driving hybrid-mediated genomic instability that promotes carcinogenesis.
source: However, our results are consistent with a different interpretation: high levels of Rad51p may be oncogenic, driving hybrid-mediated genomic instability that promotes carcinogenesis.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative interpretation based on the current findings.

claim: In vitro RecA is unable to catalyze the forward reaction with RNA.
source: Furthermore, in vitro RecA is unable to catalyze the forward reaction with RNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge from in vitro biochemical studies.

claim: Hybrid formation in trans might be a more potent promoter of genome instability than hybrid formation in cis, particularly for hybrid RNA generated from a highly repetitive element.
source: Notably, hybrid formation in trans might be a more potent promoter of genome instability than hybrid formation in cis, particularly for hybrid RNA generated from a highly repetitive element, which in trans can cause instability at a plethora of targets.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the potential impact of trans hybrid formation.

claim: Recent studies in mammalian cells and budding yeast have developed a system for generating targeted DNA breaks using the CRISPR system where target specificity is determined by a guide RNA complementary to the region of interest.
source: Intriguingly, recent studies in mammalian cells and budding yeast have developed a system for generating targeted DNA breaks using the CRISPR system, where target specificity is determined by a guide RNA complementary to the region of interest (Jinek et al., 2012; DiCarlo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CRISPR systems supported by citations.

claim: It is unknown how the guide RNA in CRISPR systems finds and hybridizes to its homologous DNA region.
source: It is unknown how the guide RNA finds and hybridizes to its homologous DNA region.
evidence: This is a statement about a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Guide RNA finding and hybridizing to homologous DNA in CRISPR could be mediated through Rad51p.
source: From our work, it is clear that these two steps could be mediated through Rad51p.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the current findings about Rad51p-mediated trans hybrid formation.

claim: Positive roles for hybrid formation in modulating transcription state have been found in both human cells and fission yeast.
source: Additionally, positive roles for hybrid formation in modulating transcription state have been found in both human cells and fission yeast (Ginno et al., 2012; Nakama et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies supported by citations.

claim: In fission yeast, there is evidence that RNA–DNA hybrids may provide a platform for RNAi-mediated heterochromatin formation, driving transcriptional silencing.
source: In fission yeast, there is evidence that RNA–DNA hybrids may provide a platform for RNAi-mediated heterochromatin formation, driving transcriptional silencing (Nakama et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on prior work in fission yeast supported by citation.

claim: If transcripts from one locus can induce hybrid formation and modulate heterochromatin formation at a homologous locus, this could provide a rapid mechanism for silencing of repetitive elements including transposable elements in a genome.
source: If transcripts from one locus can induce hybrid formation and modulate heterochromatin formation at a homologous locus, this could provide a rapid mechanism for the silencing of repetitive elements—including transposable elements—in a genome.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about potential biological implications of trans hybrid formation.

claim: Cells have developed a number of mechanisms to keep RNA–DNA hybrids in check.
source: Cells have developed a number of mechanisms to keep RNA–DNA hybrids in check.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the various anti-hybrid mechanisms described in the manuscript.

claim: Srs2p interacts directly with Rad51p, dismantling inappropriate Rad51p filaments from DNA.
source: Srs2p interacts directly with Rad51p, dismantling inappropriate Rad51p filaments from DNA (Krejci et al., 2003; Burgess et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Srs2p function supported by citations.

claim: By removing Rad51p from DNA, Srs2p could potentially inhibit hybrid formation by a mechanism like the inverse strand exchange.
source: By removing Rad51p from DNA, Srs2p could potentially inhibit hybrid formation by a mechanism like the inverse strand exchange.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic hypothesis about how Srs2p might prevent hybrid formation.

claim: Srs2p might be playing a direct role in dismantling RNA–DNA hybrids.
source: Alternatively, Srs2p might be playing a direct role in dismantling RNA–DNA hybrids.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative hypothesis about Srs2p function.

claim: The bacterial homolog of Srs2p, UvrD, has been shown to catalyze the unwinding of RNA–DNA hybrids in vitro.
source: Its bacterial homolog UvrD has been shown to catalyze the unwinding of RNA–DNA hybrids in vitro (Matson, 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge from in vitro studies on UvrD supported by citation.

claim: Cells possess at least four lines of defense against RNA–DNA hybrids: suppressing Rad51p activity by Srs2p, suppressing nuclear RNA through proper RNA biogenesis, unwinding hybrids by helicases such as Sen1p, and degrading RNA in hybrids by RNases H.
source: The work reported here, coupled with previous studies, has revealed that cells possess at least four lines of defense against RNA–DNA hybrids: (1) suppressing the deleterious hybrid-forming activity of Rad51p by Srs2p; (2) suppressing the amount of RNA in the nucleus with hybridization potential through proper RNA biogenesis; (3) unwinding RNA–DNA hybrids by helicases such as Sen1p; and (4) degrading RNA in RNA–DNA hybrids by RNases H.
evidence: This is a summary of anti-hybrid mechanisms identified in this and prior studies.

claim: Anti-hybrid pathways are not completely functionally redundant since hybrids form when any one is abrogated.
source: The fact that hybrids form when any one of these anti-hybrid pathways is abrogated clearly indicates that they are not completely functionally redundant.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that single mutations in different anti-hybrid pathways all lead to hybrid formation.

claim: The increased propensity for hybrids to form and cause instability at the rDNA locus in srs2Δ cells may be because the abundance of rRNA and homologous rDNA loci makes this region a particularly good substrate for Rad51p-mediated hybrid formation.
source: The increased propensity for hybrids to form and cause instability at the rDNA locus in srs2Δ cells is particularly intriguing, as it may be that the abundance of rRNA, as well as homologous rDNA loci, makes this region a particularly good substrate for Rad51p-mediated hybrid formation.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis to explain the high rDNA instability in srs2Δ.

claim: When Rad51p activity is no longer limiting because of inactivation of Srs2p, hybrid formation may overwhelm the anti-hybrid activities of RNases H or Sen1p.
source: When Rad51p activity is no longer limiting because of inactivation of Srs2p, hybrid formation may overwhelm the anti-hybrid activities of RNases H or Sen1p.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic hypothesis about why srs2Δ leads to hybrid accumulation.

claim: RNases H or Sen1 may be occluded from the nucleolus, making the rDNA locus more susceptible to hybrid formation by elevated Rad51p activity.
source: Alternatively, the RNases H or Sen1 may be occluded from the nucleolus, making the rDNA locus more susceptible to hybrid formation by elevated Rad51p activity.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative hypothesis about rDNA susceptibility to hybrids.
